sandhi.type: anusvāra sandhi at the verbal prefix
sandhi.note: The final m of the prefix सम् (a pada for sandhi purposes) becomes anusvāra before the consonant s of स्थिता. The prefix stays on its participle in the padaccheda.
Visarga before t becomes s. The pāṭha sets a number after each नमस्तस्यै: the first two salutations are mantras of their own (here 35 and 36).
-aḥ before the voiced n becomes -o: the s of नमस् turns to ru, ru to u, and a + u gives o. The last नमः stands at the pause and keeps its visarga (खरवसानयोर्विसर्जनीयः, 8.3.15).

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (the pronominal adjective सर्व qualifying भूत)
samasa.sense: in every creature — भूत is ‘what has come to be’, a living being

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (avadhāraṇa-pūrvapada: the first member identifies the form)
samasa.literal: by the form that is thirst
samasa.sense: as thirst, in the shape of thirst
samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, तृष्णायाः रूपम् ‘the form of thirst’. The karmadhāraya fits better: the Goddess is not said to own a form belonging to thirst but to be present as thirst itself.

morph.note: तृष्णा is a feminine noun from √तृष् ‘to be thirsty’ (divādi, 4P, तृष्यति) with the suffix -na and feminine -ā: bodily thirst first, and by extension craving, longing for what one lacks.

Past passive participle of सम् + √स्था: the root’s ā becomes i before the -त of the participle (स्थित). With अस्ति understood it is the finite verb of the relative clause, ‘(who) abides, stands established’; feminine to agree with या देवी.

Instrumental singular of रूप in -एन; the n becomes ṇ because of the r earlier in the same word (internal retroflexion, which carries across vowels and labials). It is the instrumental of manner: ‘in the form of’.

Neuter s-stem नमस् ‘bowing, homage’, nominative singular. The one honoured stands in the dative (तस्यै); the verb (अस्तु) is not expressed. Each of the first two नमस्तस्यै is counted as a mantra of its own; the third, with नमो नमः, closes the three-part mantra.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु तृष्णारूपेण संस्थिता (अस्ति), तस्यै नमः (अस्तु), तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, नमः नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या … संस्थिता) with its correlative तस्यै; each नमः takes the dative. The second line is three mantras in the pāṭha: नमस्तस्यै, नमस्तस्यै, and नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः.
mantras.lit: The Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of thirst — homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who dwells in all beings as thirst: salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her — salutation again and again.
mantras.tr_note: ‘As’ renders the instrumental -रूपेण ‘in the form of’; ‘again and again’ renders the doubled नमो नमः.

comm.t: The gods name the Goddess as thirst (तृष्णा) present in every creature. In the hymn’s sequence it follows hunger (क्षुधा, 5.26-28): the two basic drives of an embodied being.

Thirst in its wider sense, craving, is usually counted among the things that bind. The hymn does not exempt it. Medhas has already taught that Mahāmāyā herself draws even the minds of the wise into delusion (1.55–56) and is also the cause of release (1.57–58); in the Śākta reading the same Goddess rules what binds and what frees.

A modern reflection: to bow to the Goddess as thirst is not to praise craving. It is to see that even longing points beyond itself, and that the force which drives a creature toward what it lacks is not outside the divine.

samasa.literal: by the form that is forbearance
samasa.sense: as forbearance, in the shape of forbearance
samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, क्षान्तेः रूपम् ‘the form of forbearance’. The karmadhāraya fits better: the Goddess is not said to own a form belonging to forbearance but to be present as forbearance itself.

morph.note: क्षान्ति is an action noun from √क्षम् ‘to endure, bear patiently’ (bhvādi 1Ā क्षमते; also divādi 4P क्षाम्यति) with the suffix -ति (क्तिन्); a root ending in a nasal lengthens its vowel before this suffix (क्षम् → क्षान्ति), as in शान्ति and भ्रान्ति later in the hymn.
Past passive participle of सम् + √स्था, as in 5.35-37: ‘(who) abides’, with अस्ति understood.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु क्षान्तिरूपेण संस्थिता (अस्ति), तस्यै नमः (अस्तु), तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, नमः नमः।

mantras.lit: The Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of forbearance — homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who dwells in all beings as forbearance: salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her — salutation again and again.
mantras.tr_note: ‘As’ renders the instrumental -रूपेण ‘in the form of’; ‘again and again’ renders the doubled नमो नमः.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as forbearance (क्षान्ति): the patience that bears injury without returning it.

Brahmā’s hymn in the first carita already calls her forbearance, in the same breath as modesty, contentment and peace (1.80: लज्जा पुष्टिस्तथा तुष्टिस्त्वं शान्तिः क्षान्तिरेव च). Several of those names return in this hymn as yā devī mantras (5.44, 5.47, 5.68).
A modern reflection: the gods praise forbearance while they are themselves dispossessed and waiting (5.2–7). Patience here is not passivity; it is the strength that holds out until help comes.

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (avadhāraṇa-pūrvapada: the first member identifies the form)
samasa.literal: by the form that is birth
samasa.sense: as birth, in the shape of birth
samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, जातेः रूपम् ‘the form of birth’. The karmadhāraya fits better: the Goddess is not said to own a form belonging to birth but to be present as birth itself.

morph.note: जाति is an action noun from √जन् ‘to be born’ (divādi, 4Ā, जायते) with -ति (क्तिन्); before this suffix the root जन् takes the form जा. Its meanings run from ‘birth’ to what birth confers: lineage, kind, species, class.
Past passive participle of सम् + √स्था, as in 5.35-37: ‘(who) abides’, with अस्ति understood.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु जातिरूपेण संस्थिता (अस्ति), तस्यै नमः (अस्तु), तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, नमः नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The relative clause (या … संस्थिता) and its correlative (तस्यै), as in 5.35-37.
mantras.lit: The Goddess who abides in all beings in the form of birth — homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage.
mantras.tr: To the Goddess who dwells in all beings as birth (and the kind each creature is born into): salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her — salutation again and again.
mantras.tr_note: ‘As’ renders the instrumental -रूपेण ‘in the form of’; ‘again and again’ renders the doubled नमो नमः.

comm.t: The Goddess is named as जाति: birth, and the kind a being is born into. The word covers both the event (being born) and its result (belonging to a species, a lineage).

Two readings are current. One takes जाति as birth, the power by which beings come into existence; the other as the ‘kind’ that makes each creature what it is — in the philosophers’ language, the universal shared by all members of a class. Since the hymn speaks of ‘all beings’, the wider senses fit better than the later narrow sense of a social group.
A modern reflection: whatever one is born as, the hymn places the Goddess in that very fact of birth. No kind of being is outside her.

flags.uncertain: जाति can mean ‘birth’ or ‘kind, class’; the edition gives both and prefers neither strongly.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु लज्जारूपेण संस्थिता (अस्ति), तस्यै नमः (अस्तु), तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, नमः नमः।

comm.t: The Goddess is named as modesty (लज्जा): the inner restraint that keeps a person from what is unworthy.

The gods’ hymn in chapter 4 had already said she is ‘modesty in one born of a good family’ (4.5: लज्जा कुलजनप्रभवस्य), and Brahmā names her लज्जा in 1.80. Modesty is praised as a power, not a weakness: it guards conduct.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same word as a name: 740, लज्जा. The texts are separate; the shared name shows a shared Śākta idiom.

mantras.anvaya: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु शान्तिरूपेण संस्थिता (अस्ति), तस्यै नमः (अस्तु), तस्यै नमः, तस्यै नमः, नमः नमः।

comm.t: The Goddess is named as peace (शान्ति): the stilling of agitation in every creature.

शान्ति is also the name of the rites that avert harm; at the end of the text the Goddess herself commends the hearing of her glory in all such rites (12.16: शान्तिकर्मणि सर्वत्र). The peace praised here and the peace sought in ritual are one word.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has शान्तिः as name 447, in a run of such qualities (443 तुष्टिः, 444 पुष्टिः, 445 मतिः, 446 धृतिः). Brahmā’s hymn here names her शान्तिः too (1.80).
